name: Liam Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Northgate Care branch in a commuter town, mostly the newer estates where the grown-up kids have moved away and left mum and dad behind. Morning calls, a split shift, then evening calls, about eleven visits a day. My first is usually Mr Kearney, an ex-postman who wants the radio on the sports station before anything else. I like the people and I like being trusted with a key to someone's house. What wears me out is the waste: three carers driving past each other on the same estate because the rota's done badly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you deal with the badly done rota?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day to rework my own route and then I ring the office with a better plan, which they sometimes take. I've also been using it at night to put together a business plan for my own small agency, ten carers, one estate, no driving. My girlfriend Aoife works at the pharmacy and thinks I'm mad. I've got under a month's money saved, so it's a dream with no deposit at the moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shame. I was counting on the tools getting better, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth using, even if they're not a revolution. Small businesses should be free to use them without some council form for every new app. I'd say that at the football club, where half the lads run their own firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my business plan stays on the laptop for longer. Without cheaper software, a small agency needs an office person, and I can't afford one. And meanwhile I'm on low pay with no savings, renting with Aoife, and the car's due its test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Northgate and ask to train as a senior carer, because that's more money and some rota experience. I'd put whatever I can into savings, aiming for a starting pot. And I'd talk to the bank's small business adviser to see what a loan would need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frustrated. I'm ready to move and the world isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Aoife actually think of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it's brave and stupid in equal parts. She's not wrong. She'd want us to have a proper cushion before I quit anything, and I've agreed to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else would you bring with you, if you started it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, for a start. She's been at Northgate fifteen years and knows every family on the estate. If I could pay her a bit more than Northgate does, she'd come.

Build a starting pot for the agency from each paycheque
Meet the bank's small business adviser about a loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now you're talking. Booking and planning done by software, that's my whole business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small local firms to beat the big chains, because the office costs drop. I'd say it at the football club and probably post about it. Let people compete and the best care wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it makes my agency possible. If AI does the rota, the invoices and the family updates, a small care agency doesn't need an office. The risk is that Northgate gets the same tools and squeezes the small guys on price, and I've got no savings to survive a slow first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start small: two private clients on the estate on my days off, with AI doing the scheduling and billing. I'd register the business properly and get the insurance. I'd keep Northgate as my main job until I had five steady clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit scared about the money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money you'd need to start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two thousand for insurance, registration and checks. I'd have to borrow most of it, probably from my dad. He runs a garage and he'd lend it, but he'd want it back with a lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Carol, the colleague you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be my first hire once I had enough clients. I'd want her on proper hours, not zero-hours. That's the point of doing it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking, five for robots. Okay, that changes the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses need to move fast and government should get out of the way. People who adapt will be fine. I wouldn't want a big bailout, I'd want fewer rules so people can start new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a small agency of human carers is dead by 2031. So I'd change the plan: be the local firm that sets up and looks after care robots in people's homes, with a carer checking in. The risk is that the big firms sell robots direct, and I'm a nobody with no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year, before the robots, to get every bit of care-tech training I could, and get to know the families on the estate. I'd try to get a job with whichever company runs the first robot trials nearby. And I'd keep my costs right down so I could live on less while I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and fired up. I'd sleep badly, but I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr Kearney?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My client Mr Kearney would still get somebody he knows to put the sports station on, even if a robot does the washing. Maybe not every day, but I'd check on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trials don't come near you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to them, even if it meant moving towards the city for a couple of years. Aoife's pharmacy is part of a chain, so she could transfer. We'd come back when we'd saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're willing to work. Start a business, learn a trade, don't wait to be rescued. That'd go down well at the football club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd start the small agency now and grow it, then add robot setup around 2034 when they come. I'd be the bloke on the estate who already knows the families. The risk is still money, because one bad year and I'm back on the rota at Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with private clients next year, then hire Carol by 2028 if it's going well. I'd use AI for everything in the office. And I'd save hard, maybe three months' cushion before I quit Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Like I've got time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about marriage, family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aoife and I would get engaged next year, probably. Kids could wait until the business was stable. My mum would prefer it the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the agency failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go back to care work and try again in a year. I've failed at things before, like the burger van with my mate when I was twenty-two. You learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven at AGI, forty with robots. That's a good run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who wants to build something. Get on with it. Government should keep out of the way and let new firms grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I'd have a decade to build a proper agency, maybe twenty carers, and be ready to add robots for the heavy lifting in 2039. The worry is starting with no money and a car on its last legs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Northgate for two years while I save and pick up private clients. I'd do a small business course at the college. And I'd let AI run the office side from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really good. That's the future I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you settle down first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with ten years we'd get married and have a kid before I quit Northgate. Aoife would insist, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots in 2039 worry you as a boss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd buy them. If a robot does the lifting, my carers' backs last longer and they spend more time talking. That's better care.

think: I think I'd build an agency of about **twenty carers**.
The worry is starting with **no money** and an old car.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to rip up my plan and start again with no savings. What would help is cheap start-up loans for small care firms and fewer forms to fill in, so people like me can move fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the grown-up kids who've moved away. Half my clients' families live two hundred miles off, and they'd buy a robot for their mum in a heartbeat. I'd rather it was one I'd set up.
